caption:
Former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner told investors his hedge fund lost 65% after fees in the third quarter, the WSJ reported.
In July, AI stocks fell, lenders made margin calls and the fund sold most of its stocks to Citadel.
It is still up 88.5% for 2026 and wants to short and borrow again.

paragraphs.text: Situational Awareness, the hedge fund run by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, told investors it lost 65% after fees in the third quarter of 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported on November 25, citing an investor letter. Reuters, which relayed the report, said it could not immediately verify it, and the firm did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Even after that loss, the fund was up 88.5% after fees for the year through September, according to the same report. Aschenbrenner launched the fund in 2024, Reuters said, after working as a researcher at OpenAI.

Most of the damage came in July. In a letter to investors at the end of that month, the fund said its portfolio had fallen 67% as AI stocks dropped, while it was still up 80% for 2026 at that point, Reuters reported on July 31, 2026. The letter described those figures as an unaudited estimate, according to a copy published by Business Insider.

The letter said the fund had come closer to permanent capital impairment than it found acceptable and told investors, "We let you down this month." It described the pressure on the fund as "essentially similar to a bank run," according to Reuters.

Business Insider reported that the sharp drop in tech stocks triggered a series of margin calls on the fund's leveraged positions. The fund then sold the bulk of its public stock portfolio to Ken Griffin's Citadel. Business Insider said the fund held assets worth $45 billion at its peak and fell to about $10 billion in a matter of days.

The fund did not step away from AI. It kept its stake in Anthropic ahead of that company's stock market debut, Business Insider reported on November 17. A regulatory filing covering positions as of September 30 showed the remaining public book concentrated in AI-linked names, with SharonAI at 28% of the fund, Bloom Energy at 24.7%, Nebius at 21.1%, SanDisk at 11.5% and a Roundhill memory ETF at 8.9%. Much of that exposure was held through call options rather than shares.

After Anthropic's public offering, the portfolio is split roughly 70% publicly traded stocks and 30% positions in private companies, according to the Journal's account of the letter. Aschenbrenner expects the fund to start shorting stocks again and possibly to resume trading with borrowed money, though at lower levels than before, the report said.

The numbers show how a fund can be up sharply for the year and still suffer a near collapse along the way. Leverage magnified the gains in the first half and then forced sales when prices turned, which is why the plan to borrow again, even at lower levels, is the detail investors are likely to weigh most closely.

The fund is also one of the most visible bets on the idea that AI will keep reshaping markets quickly. A 65% quarterly loss followed by a return to concentrated AI positions makes it a running test of that view, with the outcome tied closely to how AI stocks and Anthropic's shares perform.
Watch whether Situational Awareness restarts shorting and leverage in the coming months, and how its stake in Anthropic moves as that stock trades after its November debut.
